newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: HOWARD DEFENDS OVERSEAS TRIP
The Prime Minister, John Howard, has defended his two week overseas trip against claims he should be at home tackling the unemployment problem.
Both the Federal Opposition and Independent Pauling Hanson have levelled the criticism at the Prime Minister.
However Mr Howard says his visit to Britain and the United States is serving the national interest and will help secure jobs.
The Prime Minister says in both coutries he'll be highlighting the strengths of the Australian economy.
Mr Howard also says his visit will address criticisms at home and in the British media about Australia's treatment of its indigenous people.
HILL SAYS GREENHOUSE TARGETS NOT THE ANSWER

Federal Environment Minister Robert Hill says Australia's mineral processing industries will be pushed offshore if uniform global targets for reducing greenhouse emissions are introduced. Senator Hill will attend the Earth Summit in New York next week, which is likely to renew calls for uniform targets but Australia is opposed to the plan because of fears it will devastate the coal and mining industries.
He says better global outcomes will not be achieved by transferring those industries to less efficient producers.
Senator Hill says if the mineral processing sector is forced offshore then Australians will lose jobs but there's no guarantee the environment will be better off.
He says the outcomes could be worse if the fuel sources offshore are more polluting than the ones being offered by Australia.
ACTU ACCUSES GOVT OF BLAMING VICTIMS
ACTU President Jenny George says a lack of government vision and proactive policies is leading the Howard Government to a "blame the victim" strategy.
Ms George has told a national conference on unemployment it is an approach that's likely to grow further.
The Federal government is planning to introduce a Common Youth Allowance and scrap the dole for 16 and 17 year olds while applying a parental means test to those in the 18 to 20 age group.
Ms George says while the move will improve the unemployment statistics by removing the 16 and 17 year olds, it will mean struggling families will be forced to endure even more hardship. - - - -
FATALITY AT MT ISA MINES
A truck driver has been killed in an above-ground accident at MIM's mine in Mount Isa this morning, bringing to five the number of fatalities at the site in just over a year.
Police are still investigating the incident that happened when the man was apparently loading scrap metal at the mine's dump site.
The man was not an MIM employee and police believe he could have been from interstate.
The last fatal accident at the site occurred only two weeks ago when the driver of a haulage unit was killed when the unit fell into a mined pit.
After that accident MIM Executive General Manager Stephen O'Donnell said the company's safety record was not up to the required standard.
REPORT EXPRESSES CONCERN FOR NEW MOTHERS
There must be adequate community care for new mothers if their hospital stays are going to be shortened according to the author of a new report on Australian mothers.
The report, entitled Australia's Mothers and Babies 1994, has found three in ten new mothers stay in hospital for fewer than four days after giving birth.
The report has been compiled by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and Director of Perinatal Statistics, Dr Paul Lancaster, says many women feel four days is not long enough.
Dr Lancaster says surveys have shown most women believe a hospital stay of five to six days is necessary to recover from the birth and begin caring for and breastfeeding a new baby.

The report also reveals the average age of first time mothers is at an all-time high at just over 26-years of age...and the number of births to young mothers aged less-than-17 is up 10-percent in 12-months.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
